reason: The judgment held only that this particular agreement made damages the substitute remedy and contained no sale-compulsion clause, so the statement is ambiguous and underqualified.
The court relied on the principle that specific performance is discretionary and not to be granted or refused capriciously.
The contractual-variation rule is supported and ratio, but the claimed Civil Procedure Code section was not the provision construed for that rule.
The notary's attestation was treated as a supporting fact on acceptance, not as an independent rule or holding.
The court accepted minor acceptance in this beneficial gift context, but the statement drops the judgment's minor-capacity and donor-revocation qualifications.
This is a generic observation rather than a legal rule decided by the court, and the quote does not support it.
The court's revocability holding was expressly subject to statutory exceptions and execution by a lawful written instrument, which the statement omits.
Temple gifts were only listed as a statutory exception and the statement omits the specific vesting conditions, so it is not this case's operative ratio.
The court held that describing a Kandyan gift as irrevocable was not an express renunciation of the statutory right to revoke.
The court discussed damages under section 49, but the absolute 'only remedy' wording drops the acknowledged revision and restitutio jurisdiction in appropriate cases.
The no-prejudice point depended on the statutory damages charge, so stated generally it is materially overbroad.
The refusal of extraordinary relief rested on the petitioners' lack of due diligence after surveyor notice and their acceptance of the decree's finality.
The one-year limit applied to a possessory action under section 4 of the Prescription Ordinance, not to plaintiffs generally.
The restoration-without-title rule under section 4 depends on proof of dispossession otherwise than by process of law within one year, which is omitted.
The point was ratio for section 66 land-dispute proceedings, but the statement overstates it as applying to Primary Courts Procedure Act actions generally.
The court set aside the partition proceedings because the corpus was not identified and a larger land was accepted without the required process.
The court applied the rule that a partition decree cannot be entered by settlement because the judge must investigate title and shares.
The holding was that the acts taken as a whole were nuisance under section 22(2)(d) of the Rent Act, but the statement omits both qualifications.
The court held intention irrelevant only where the tenant knowingly did the acts under section 22(2)(d), which the statement does not preserve.
The duty belonged to the propounder of a contested Last Will when suspicious circumstances arose, not to any party generally.
The appeal failed because the propounder did not lead evidence dispelling the suspicions surrounding the Last Will.
The court treated the proctor's evidence as insufficient by itself to establish testamentary capacity amid suspicious circumstances.
The court held that the overdraft contract was proved despite missing written requests caused by the 1983 riots and other evidence established the facility.
The court held prescription did not defeat the bank's claim because the debt had been acknowledged and demand was made before action.
The actual holding concerned tacit admission of a specific trust receipt by the defendant firm, not a general rule that any tacit admission proves a fact.
